world_bible.story_framework: Near-future hard sci-fi salvage drama. Juno Arak, a salvage pilot working the debris belt around gas giant Tessaly, must investigate the disappearance of her mentor Captain Odile Marsh after a single last transmission — 'Lantern'. Conflicts: corporate pressure (Ostrander Mining Concern) to seal Meridian-9 vs. scavenger cults and survivors; salvage economics and life-support/time pressure; unraveling Meridian-9's secrets and Odile's fate. Narrative threads: investigating Meridian-9, navigating politics with Director Hal Voren and Brother Calix, protecting/repairing the Kestrel while managing scarce resources, and interpreting Odile's logs/clues.
world_bible.world_mechanics: Grounded hard-SF rules. No magic. Life support, oxygen, and hull integrity are mechanically consequential; EV (extravehicular) time is limited by suit O2 and suit integrity. Salvage yields credits but attracts corporate and cult attention. Communications are imperfect across the debris belt; data slates can be corrupted. Robotics exist but are fallible (maintenance bots like Mox can be damaged or reprogrammed). Physical hazards: micro-debris, radiation pockets near the gas giant, volatile hull ruptures, and failing docking rings. Resource management (O2, fuel, spare parts, credits) and realistic physics (momentum, limited thruster delta-v for the tug) determine success.
world_bible.narrative_style: Grounded, tense, close third-person with documentary fragments (log entries, survey data). Sparse, technical prose interleaved with atmospheric descriptions of the gas giant and derelict station interiors. Stakes communicated through time pressure and resource scarcity rather than supernatural elements.

known_characters.name: Juno Arak
known_characters.description: Protagonist. Salvage pilot of the tug Kestrel. Practical, determined, emotionally tethered to mentor Odile. Skilled at short-range salvage ops and EVA work.

known_characters.name: Captain Odile Marsh
known_characters.description: Juno's mentor and veteran survey captain who vanished three weeks ago while surveying Meridian-9. Last transmission: 'Lantern'. Left behind a brass compass and survey logs.

known_characters.name: Priya Sen
known_characters.description: Kestrel's engineer. Sarcastic, fiercely loyal to Juno, expert at jury-rigging and repairing damaged kit. Currently assisting Juno in inspecting the hull for potential weaknesses.

known_characters.name: Brother Calix
known_characters.description: Leader of a scavenger cult living in the belt. Charismatic and territorial; the cult reveres salvaged artifacts and opposes corporate sealing of sites.

known_characters.name: Director Hal Voren
known_characters.description: Head of the Ostrander Mining Concern. Corporate, pragmatic, pushing to seal Meridian-9 to protect assets and interests.

known_characters.name: Mox
known_characters.description: A damaged maintenance robot that follows Juno. Limited autonomy and patchwork repairs; useful for heavy lifting and diagnostics but unreliable under stress.

known_characters.name: Dr. Ilse Brandt
known_characters.description: Scientist who survived on Meridian-9. Potential source of firsthand information and technical insight into the station's research and failure.

known_locations.name: Kestrel
known_locations.description: Juno's small salvage tug. Modular cargo bay, jury-rigged life support, patched hull. Currently adrift with failing reactor output and life support. The hull has fresh scoring and a shallow crease along the cargo-bay plating, but the seam is still closed with no puncture or signs of escaping air.

known_locations.name: Meridian-9 docking ring
known_locations.description: The external docking and transfer hub of the derelict research station Meridian-9. The control display is dark, and the conduit is now exposed with the plate cut free and shifted aside, revealing the coupling under strain.

known_locations.name: Meridian-9 hydroponics deck
known_locations.description: Interior deck of Meridian-9 used for plant growth and life-support research. The breach cut in the sealed bulkhead is venting gas into the passage, making the route beyond unsafe to enter.

known_locations.name: Ostrander refinery
known_locations.description: Processing facility run by Ostrander Mining Concern. Heavy machinery, secure storage, and corporate presence in the belt. Juno has docked among the facility’s service traffic and is navigating through the public access corridor.

known_locations.name: Vigil
known_locations.description: The cult's shrine-ship. A patched-together vessel where Brother Calix and the scavenger cult live and store relics. Juno has docked here to negotiate for a stolen navigation core.

known_locations.name: Port Halcyon
known_locations.description: Crowded trade hub and supply node for the belt. Market for salvage goods, pawnshops, and places to pick up leads or contentious orders. Juno has arrived with the Kestrel, surrounded by dock traffic and market noise.

known_locations.name: Tessaly cloud skimmer platform
known_locations.description: Floating platform that samples Tessaly's upper atmosphere. Juno has arrived and is holding position beside its instruments, tuning the receiver to Odile’s beacon signal. A service access hatch is visible along the platform’s outer structure.

known_locations.name: old docks
known_locations.description: The abandoned docking area away from the Kestrel, where Juno leads the guards to identify the stash location.

known_items.name: plasma cutter
known_items.description: Handheld cutting tool used for cutting hull plating and salvage rigs. Essential for boarding and salvage operations. Now secured against Juno's suit.

known_items.name: cracked data slate with Odile's survey logs
known_items.description: Damaged slate containing Odile Marsh's last survey data and voice notes. Sold at Port Halcyon pawnshop.

known_items.name: brass compass (Odile's)
known_items.description: Old-fashioned brass compass that belonged to Odile. Currently held by Brother Calix.

known_items.name: portable O2 canister
known_items.description: Spare emergency oxygen supply for short EV excursions and suit top-ups. Now activated, but the gas is escaping without forming mist.

known_items.name: Mox (unit)
known_items.description: Damaged maintenance robot unit that follows Juno and can be utilized for repairs and heavy tasks.

known_items.name: compact survey drone
known_items.description: A small drone used for surveying, now confirmed to have no visible manual control or override. The casing remains intact, but it is inert, with a dark status lamp and a damaged rotor, rendering it non-functional.

known_items.name: navigation core
known_items.description: Essential component for the Kestrel's navigation system, allowing safe operation in the debris belt. Now installed and operational.

known_items.name: Kestrel Hull Integrity
known_items.description: The hull integrity is stabilized at 67 percent, with braces supporting the damaged section but not repairing the scored plating.

known_items.name: compact beacon unit
known_items.description: A compact beacon unit fixed to the platform’s internal frame. Its status light pulses steadily, and the relay clicks in time with each signal burst. The casing is intact, and it is transmitting without any visible faults.

currentState.current_task: Check the skimmer's instruments for navigation logs or systems that might have recorded the beacon's frequency or recent activity.

chatHistory.text:
Juno turns the beacon under the service light and inspects the casing, seams, and exposed contacts. She finds no readable label, manufacturer mark, or visible serial number. The unit has no directional indicator or additional control that would identify where its signal is going.

She checks the receiver beside the beacon again. The reading is strongest close to the casing, but it provides no bearing or destination. The relay keeps clicking in its steady rhythm, and the status light continues to pulse. Nothing on the beacon itself identifies its origin or offers a way to trace the signal farther. Juno is left with the receiver in hand beside the active unit.
I use the receiver to scan for any nearby signals or devices that might help me trace the beacon's origin.

Juno holds the receiver away from the beacon and scans the platform’s nearby signal range. The display shifts through brief traces as she checks around the service passage and the skimmer’s instruments.

One signal remains steady: the compact beacon behind her. The receiver catches no second transmission or device response that could identify the beacon’s origin. When Juno turns back toward the beacon, its reading strengthens; as she angles away, it fades. The receiver still gives no bearing or destination.

The beacon continues to pulse and click at the same rate. Juno stands beside the platform’s instruments with the receiver tuned to its signal.
I check the skimmer's instruments for any navigation logs or systems that might have recorded the beacon's frequency or recent activity.

Juno checks the skimmer’s instrument housings, moving from one control face to the next. The displays show atmospheric sampling data and platform status. She searches the available records for radio activity, beacon frequencies, or recent signal events.

The stored entries concern the skimmer’s own sampling operations. None lists the compact beacon or records its transmission. The instruments provide no linked navigation log and show no connection to the beacon’s relay. Its pulse continues steadily behind her, while the receiver still gives only a stronger reading near the unit.

Juno is beside the skimmer’s instrument panel with the active beacon still transmitting in the service passage.

unprocessedArchive.text:
Juno leans close to the beacon and examines the casing, contacts, and relay under the platform’s service lighting. The casing is intact. The contacts are clean beneath the secured cover, and the wiring shows no visible breaks, loose connections, or added components.

The relay clicks in time with each burst. The status light pulses steadily. Nothing appears damaged or irregular, and the signal gives no sign of interference at the unit.

Juno replaces the cover and checks the receiver beside the beacon. It registers the strongest reading at close range. The beacon continues transmitting at the same level, with no visible fault to repair. The receiver is in her hand beside the active unit.
I move away from the beacon and search the platform for any nearby control panels or equipment that might enhance the signal reception.

Juno leaves the beacon and searches the platform’s accessible service area. She checks the skimmer’s visible instrument housings and the structures near the service passage, looking for a control panel or equipment connected to the beacon’s transmission.

The platform’s sampling instruments are present, but she finds no control marked for the beacon and no separate relay or signal amplifier. The beacon remains the only visible transmitter. Its steady pulse carries through the receiver, but the reading weakens as Juno moves farther from it.

She stops beside the platform’s instruments with the receiver still tuned. The beacon is behind her in the passage; nothing nearby offers a way to increase its reception.
I return to the beacon and position the receiver as close as possible to it to strengthen the signal.

Juno returns through the service passage to the beacon. She brings the receiver close to the casing and holds it beside the pulsing status light, keeping the antenna clear of the frame.

The reading rises to its strongest level at close range. The relay continues clicking with each burst, and the beacon’s pulse remains steady. The receiver is picking up the signal more clearly here, but the beacon itself does not change output.

Juno shifts the receiver a short distance around the casing. The reading drops as she moves away from the unit. She brings it back beside the beacon, where the signal is strongest. The transmission remains steady, and its source is still not identified.
I examine the beacon for any labels or markings that might indicate its origin or any features that could help me trace the signal further.
